scoreNote: Strong (5): rejects the absolute claim with two strong reasons — means cause real harm and corrupt the ends they serve — then concedes the limited truth before reaffirming the position; tightly reasoned.

sentences.text: It is a seductive idea that a noble enough end can excuse whatever it takes to reach it, and history is littered with crimes committed in the name of good causes.
The statement embraces this logic fully, holding that if a goal is worthy, then any means taken to attain it are justifiable.
I strongly disagree, because the means we use have consequences and a moral weight of their own, and a worthy goal pursued through monstrous means is neither worthy nor truly achieved.
First, no end exists in isolation, and the means used to reach it produce consequences of their own.
To pursue a good goal through violence, deceit, or cruelty is to create real suffering now in exchange for a benefit that is only hoped for later.
Revolutions launched to free people have, through terror and bloodshed, produced tyrannies worse than the ones they replaced.
The harm done by the means is certain and immediate, while the worthy end is often distant and unsure, so any means trades guaranteed evil for speculative good.
A doctor does not cure a patient by killing him, and a society does not achieve justice by committing injustice along the way.
History's bloodiest chapters were written by people convinced that their cause excused the carnage.
Because means cause real harm, they cannot be excused merely by pointing at a distant goal.
Moreover, immoral means tend to corrupt the very goal they were meant to serve.
A cause defended through lies becomes a cause built on lies, and the habits formed in pursuing it do not vanish once the goal is reached.
A movement for freedom that wins through terror tends to keep ruling through terror, because the people and methods that triumph are the ones the struggle has shaped.
Means are not neutral tools laid down at the finish line; they become part of whatever is built.
The end never quite arrives pure, because it carries within it everything done to attain it.
To say the goal justifies any means is to forget that the means become the goal.

sections.role: Body — The kernel of truth and its limit

sentences.text: Admittedly, there is a limited truth buried in the statement.
Worthy goals do sometimes justify difficult or costly means — a just war, a painful sacrifice, a hard compromise — that would be wrong in the absence of any purpose.
But this is a far cry from any means, which would license torture, murder, and betrayal whenever the cause seemed grand enough.
The honest principle is that a worthy end can justify some means and never others, and that the more monstrous the means, the worthier the end must be even to be debated.
The worthier the goal, the more tempting it becomes to forgive ourselves anything done in its name.
Any is precisely the word that turns a reasonable idea into a dangerous one.
In conclusion, a worthy goal can justify some means but never any means whatever.
Because means cause real harm and shape the ends they serve, the word any makes the statement an invitation to atrocity dressed up as idealism.
The worthiness of a goal is a reason to choose our means with more care, not less.
